title: Rethinking Tool Design for Agentic RCA: A Controlled Empirical Study
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly explored for root cause analysis (RCA) in microservice systems, where diagnosis requires extracting useful evidence from massive metric streams. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed preprocessing or predefined toolsets, leaving limited empirical guidance on how RCA tools should be designed and combined. We conduct a controlled empirical study of tool design in agentic RCA, examining tool abstraction and composition together with model capability and microservice system complexity. We organize the study around a four level RCA tool spectrum: L0 provides no structured RCA tools and allows Python based analysis, while L1, L2, and L3 provide metric access, evidence analysis, and diagnostic methods, respectively. We implement 24 structured RCA tools across L1–L3 and evaluate 7 tool configurations, 4 models spanning distinct capability levels, and 375 failure cases from 3 microservice environments: Online Boutique, Sock Shop, and Train Ticket. Our results show that tool utility is nonmonotonic: higher abstraction and richer toolsets do not consistently improve diagnostic effectiveness or efficiency. More strikingly, L3 level tools can hurt weaker models but become increasingly beneficial as model capability improves. Tool configuration rankings also shift across microservice environments, showing that no single toolset remains optimal across different system profiles. Overall, our study provides a systematic empirical basis for RCA tool design and practical guidance for matching tool abstraction and composition to model capability and system complexity.

levels.name: Agent-written analysis
levels.output: Results of the agent's own programs
levels.tool: Execute Python over the same case metrics, incident context, and service topology.
levels.agent: Choose, implement, and interpret the entire analysis. There are no predefined RCA procedures.

diagram.result: Results of the agent's own programs
diagram.remaining: Choose, implement, and interpret the analysis.
diagram.visual_description: A code editor and a computed time series.

levels.name: Metric access
levels.tool: Retrieve metric samples, summary statistics, metric ownership, and local service dependencies.
levels.agent: Choose what to inspect, identify unusual behavior, and reason about its cause. These tools do not score anomalies or rank root causes.

diagram.remaining: Find unusual behavior and reason about its cause.
diagram.visual_description: A selected time window and a basic summary, without anomaly scores or cause rankings.

capabilities: Mean, maximum, minimum, sum, and percentiles

levels.name: Evidence analysis
levels.tool: Analyze time series and return anomaly scores, change points, candidate metrics, temporal features, and evidence graphs.
levels.agent: Relate evidence across services and decide what it means for diagnosis. The most anomalous metric is not necessarily the root cause.

diagram.result: Anomalies, change points, and evidence links
diagram.remaining: Connect the evidence. Distinguish symptoms from causes.
diagram.visual_description: An anomaly marker on a time series and a graph of related evidence.

capabilities: Anomaly detection: 3-sigma, IQR, MAD, ESD, SPOT
Change points: CUSUM, PELT, binary segmentation, Page–Hinkley

levels.name: Diagnostic methods
levels.tool: Generate candidate rankings, combine diagnostic evidence, and assemble explanations for specified candidates.
levels.agent: Assess whether to keep or revise the recommendations, then submit the final candidate list and failure type.

diagram.remaining: Assess the recommendation, then keep or revise it.
diagram.visual_description: An ordered candidate list beside its supporting evidence relationships, not a final diagnosis.

capabilities: Graph ranking: PageRank, personalized PageRank, random walk with restart
Classic RCA: MonitorRank, CloudRanger, MicroRCA, Microscope, MicroCause, MicroHECL
Fusion of anomaly, ranking, topology, and timing evidence

spectrum_example.task: A ticketing request becomes slow. What does each interface give the agent?
spectrum_example.notice: Schematic outputs, not a recorded benchmark trace. Sample values are illustrative; no measured anomaly score or diagnostic confidence is implied.

L0.label: Agent-written Python · one analysis step
lines: output: 83.0 ms · computed by the agent's code
L0.meaning: Even this summary requires agent-written code. The agent implements any further analysis itself; no ready-made RCA procedure is provided.

L1.label: Metric query and summary
L1.meaning: These are measurements and summaries. The interface has not labeled them anomalous or named a root cause.

L2.label: Anomaly and relationship analysis
lines: auth latency: change detected near the incident
L2.meaning: This identifies unusual signals and their relationships. Highest anomaly rank does not mean most likely root cause.

L3.label: Diagnostic ranking and explanation
lines: support: latency evidence and service relationships
agent still submits the final entity and fault type
L3.meaning: This is a diagnostic recommendation, not the final answer. The agent must assess the support before keeping or revising it.

reporting.detail: Seven structured configurations plus an independent L0 reference. Qwen3.7-Plus is tested under all eight; the other three models under L0, L1, L1+L2, and L1+L2+L3.

The configurations share case data, the agent harness, the task prompt, and execution limits. Available structured interfaces and their instructions change. Shared data does not imply identical available actions.

L0 explicitly exposes a general Python execution interface. The manuscript does not explicitly say whether structured configurations also expose it, or list the sandbox restrictions and installed dependencies.

Accuracy covers all evaluated cases, including invalid or missing diagnoses. Token usage includes input and output across all LLM calls; token, latency, and API cost are averaged over all evaluated cases.
Repeat counts, random seeds, and uncertainty intervals are not stated. Small differences should not be read as statistically established improvements.

The 79% / 5% / 5% comparison concerns switches from an L3 candidate to a different entity ranked most anomalous by L2. The corresponding sample counts are not stated; these percentages are not overall tool accuracy.

models.name: Qwen3-8B
models.note: L3 is available, but almost never called. The larger action space accompanies longer trajectories and more invalid actions; this is not evidence that incorrect L3 outputs mislead the model.

models.name: Qwen3-32B
models.note: The model calls L3 but overrides roughly one third of its correct recommendations. Tool availability, correct use, and sound assessment are separate requirements.

models.name: Qwen3-235B-A22B
models.note: Most trajectories invoke L3, but only about half obtain a ranking. Narrowing the incident window can discard useful evidence; invoking a tool does not guarantee a useful result.

models.name: Qwen3.7-Plus
models.note: This model performs its strongest top-1 localization with its own Python analysis. Additional tools can improve failure typing, while candidate revisions remain a source of localization errors.

systems.name: Online Boutique
systems.note: When an agent switches from an L3 candidate to a different entity ranked highest by L2, the switch is correct in 79% of those cases.

systems.name: Sock Shop
systems.note: In the same conditional analysis, switches to a different L2-ranked entity are correct in only 5% of cases.

systems.name: Train Ticket
systems.structure: Synchronous and asynchronous communication with complex call chains
systems.note: Switches to a different L2-ranked entity are correct in only 5% of cases. Service count alone does not explain this contrast.

audit.title: Two services. An unresolved diagnosis.
audit.evidence: The reported investigation examines ts-auth-service and the payment service. The true faulty service and fault type are not shown to the agent here.
audit.interpretation: The diagnosis is open. No candidate has yet been ranked in this summary.
audit.check: Keep the agent's observations separate from the benchmark label, which is revealed after the decision.
audit.caption: A summary of the reported case, not a raw tool transcript. The reasoning checks are explanatory commentary on this page.

audit.title: L3 ranks auth first.
audit.evidence: The diagnostic tool ranks ts-auth-service as the top root cause candidate.
audit.interpretation: Auth is the current leading recommendation; payment is not the top L3 candidate.
audit.check: A candidate ranking is a hypothesis to assess, not ground truth. Any revision still needs relevant evidence.
audit.caption: The tool has proposed a cause. The agent must decide whether the available evidence supports keeping or revising it.

audit.title: L2 highlights payment memory.
audit.evidence: Candidate filtering ranks a memory metric of the payment service highest.
audit.interpretation: The agent now has a prominent payment anomaly alongside the auth recommendation.
audit.check: An anomaly ranking answers where a signal is unusual. It does not establish which service caused the incident.
audit.caption: L2 and L3 answer different questions. The new signal alone does not justify replacing the root cause candidate.

audit.title: Missing symptoms become a reason to reject.
audit.evidence: The agent finds no CPU or memory anomaly in auth, while observing its latency.
audit.interpretation: The agent treats auth latency as a propagated symptom and shifts suspicion toward payment.
audit.check: No CPU or memory anomaly does not rule out a delay fault. Nor does it show that auth latency propagated from payment.
audit.caption: The unsupported step is the interpretation: absence of these symptoms is used to dismiss a different kind of fault.

audit.title: The agent switches to payment.
audit.evidence: Payment has the highest-ranked memory anomaly; auth lacks a CPU or memory anomaly. No new L3 ranking is reported here.
audit.interpretation: The agent blames payment instead of ts-auth-service.
audit.check: The revision combines two observations, but neither establishes payment as the cause or rules out auth. A worse-looking metric is not enough.
audit.caption: Inspect the reason for the switch, not only which tool was consulted. The benchmark answer is revealed next.

audit.title: The root cause was auth, not payment.
audit.evidence_title: Benchmark label · revealed after the decision
audit.evidence: Root cause entity: ts-auth-service. Injected failure type: delay. This label is available to the reader for the audit, not to the diagnosing agent.
audit.interpretation: The agent's payment diagnosis is incorrect. In this case, the original L3 recommendation matched the true faulty service.
audit.check: Do not conclude that L3 should always be trusted. Require fault-relevant evidence that supports a new candidate and distinguishes it from the old one.
audit.caption: The lesson is evidence-based revision, not unconditional trust in a diagnostic tool.

guidelines.title: Separate the two diagnostic targets.
guidelines.when: A tool addition helps one accuracy metric but hurts another.
guidelines.check: Compare first-choice root cause accuracy, fault type accuracy, and cost separately.
guidelines.try: Choose the target you need to improve before selecting a configuration; report the tradeoff rather than a single winner.

guidelines.title: Match tools to demonstrated capability.
guidelines.when: Tools are available, but the agent gains little from them.
guidelines.check: Measure selection, valid calls, useful returned results, and whether correct recommendations survive the final decision.
guidelines.try: Simplify the failing interface or its instructions; evaluate result assessment separately from tool invocation.

guidelines.title: Make candidate revisions accountable.
guidelines.when: New observations cause the agent to replace a diagnostic candidate.
guidelines.check: Record the old candidate, new candidate, and evidence supporting the change or contradicting the old explanation.
guidelines.try: Ask for fault-relevant evidence before a switch; do not equate the most anomalous metric with the root cause.

guidelines.title: Distinguish the fault from its symptoms.
guidelines.when: The entity is right, but the predicted fault type is wrong.
guidelines.check: Look for evidence that separates competing fault types, rather than only the most prominent CPU or latency symptom.
guidelines.try: Expose fault-specific observations and ask the agent to compare alternative explanations.

guidelines.title: Revalidate when the system changes.
guidelines.when: A configuration is moved to a different microservice environment.
guidelines.check: Re-evaluate accuracy and whether anomaly rankings align with labeled root causes in that environment.
guidelines.try: Validate the configuration locally before transferring its ranking from another system.

guidelines.title: Repair the stage that actually fails.
guidelines.when: Diagnosis fails, despite adding more tools or evidence.
guidelines.check: Classify the failure: invalid execution, missing cause, wrong candidate decision, or wrong fault type.
guidelines.try: Improve interface reliability, evidence coverage, candidate comparison, or fault-specific evidence according to that failure.
